title: Why opportunity should become the new measure of university success
summary:
Degrees are no longer enough. In an AI-driven economy, universities will be judged by the opportunities they help create.

The post Why opportunity should become the new measure of university success appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
HEPI is recruiting our first Communications Manager. In this exciting role, you will help shape how we share our research, events and ideas. Visit this webpage for the full job description and details of how to apply. Deadline 26th July.

This blog was kindly authored by Professor Paul M. Marshall, Vice-President (Global Campus) and Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Careers & Enterprise) at the University of East London.

The UK higher education sector is currently focused on financial sustainability, international recruitment and public confidence. These debates really matter. But they risk obscuring a more fundamental question.

Are universities still organised for the economy that now exists?

I was reminded of this recently while speaking at New York Tech Week. The audience included founders, investors, employers, policymakers and innovators from both sides of the Atlantic. Discussions ranged from AI and fintech to customer experience and international expansion.

What struck me was that nobody was talking about degrees.

Investors talked about talent.

Founders talked about talent.

Employers talked about talent.

The discussion was not about qualifications. It was about how to attract talented people, develop them, connect them to opportunity and help them adapt in an economy being reshaped by AI and technological change.

Yet much of higher education still behaves as though the degree itself is the end product. We recruit students. We deliver programmes. We award degrees. We celebrate graduation.

Meanwhile, employers recruit globally. Skills requirements evolve continuously. Careers are increasingly non-linear. Innovation happens through networks rather than institutions. The world has changed. Many universities have not changed with it. This matters because the pressures facing the sector are not simply financial. They are strategic.

Universities cannot simply cut their way to long-term sustainability. Nor can they rely indefinitely on recruiting from the same markets using the same models. The institutions that thrive over the next decade will be those that remain indispensable to students, employers and society.

That requires a broader understanding of what universities are for. Historically, universities have provided access to education. Increasingly, they must also help provide access to opportunity. That may sound like a subtle distinction. I believe it is becoming one of the defining challenges facing higher education. For much of their history, universities built campuses and asked students to come to them. Increasingly, I believe the future works the other way around. Universities need to build networks that connect talent, employers, entrepreneurs, investors and opportunity wherever people happen to be.

That is not simply a question of international recruitment. Indeed, I think the sector still talks about internationalisation too often as though recruitment is the objective. It is not. Recruitment is a mechanism. The objective should be building long-term talent, employer and innovation networks that create value for students, employers and society. That is where internationalisation, employability and economic growth increasingly converge.

At the University of East London, this thinking sits behind our Global Campus strategy. Two weeks ago, we launched UEL USA in Miami. The significance of that launch was not the opening of an overseas office. It was the creation of new pathways connecting students, employers, entrepreneurs, investors and innovators across multiple markets. The same principle underpins our partnership with the Tampa Bay Wave in Florida. The lesson is broader than any individual institution. The real opportunity lies in building enduring connections between education, employment, enterprise and investment. Bringing this to life, in a few weeks time, 20 UEL students will embark upon a two month work placement with companies in the Tampa Bay Wave ecosystem. Building a genuine economic and innovation bridge between London and Tampa.

This shift has important implications for policy and institutional strategy. If opportunity becomes as important as education, employability can no longer be treated as a service students discover in their final year. Entrepreneurship cannot remain a peripheral activity. Alumni engagement cannot be viewed as something that begins after graduation. Instead, universities need to think much more deliberately about how they connect learners to employers, mentors, professional development, enterprise support and lifelong learning opportunities throughout their careers. At UEL, this thinking sits behind CareerVerse, a digital careers and entrepreneurship ecosystem designed to connect students and graduates to opportunities over the long term. The platform itself is not the point. The principle is. In a world increasingly shaped by AI, access to opportunity may become just as important as access to education. That has profound implications for how universities are organised, funded and evaluated. It also changes how we think about outcomes.

Universities should continue to be judged on academic quality, research excellence and student experience. But I believe they should increasingly be judged on the opportunities they help create. Not only for graduates, but for employers, entrepreneurs and communities.

At UEL, our graduates now rank second in the United Kingdom for graduate start-up creation and twentieth nationally for graduate company employment. These outcomes matter because universities should not simply produce graduates who seek opportunity. They should produce founders, innovators, employers and problem-solvers who create opportunity for others. The economic and social impact of those individuals extends far beyond the university itself. If policymakers are serious about productivity, economic growth and social mobility, then higher education policy needs to move beyond a narrow focus on participation and attainment. Those goals remain important. But the next challenge is ensuring that people can translate education into opportunity throughout their lives.

That means encouraging stronger employer partnerships, supporting innovation ecosystems, rewarding entrepreneurial activity and recognising the value of lifelong engagement between universities and learners.

The question is no longer whether universities provide access to education. Most do that reasonably well. The more important question is whether universities can provide access to opportunity. In an economy increasingly shaped by AI, global labour markets and rapid technological change, that may become the defining measure of institutional success. It is also where the future value of higher education will increasingly be found.

title: What universities count – and what they cannot afford to ignore

The post What universities count – and what they cannot afford to ignore appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Anna Zimdars, Christopher Playford, Eve Worth, Luke Graham, Joanna Merrett and Joseph Crawford, members of the Centre for Social Mobility, University of Exeter.

He that breaks a thing to find out what it is has left the path of wisdom.

— J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring

UK higher education is under acute pressure. Senior leaders face difficult decisions shaped by frozen fees, rising costs, underfunded research, volatile international recruitment and the legacy of shifting universities from a public good towards a private good within a market logic.

Yet those pressures do not fall evenly, and they do not determine a single institutional response. Each university has its own historic, financial and regional story as well as a strategy and vision for what it wants to be. Sector pressures are real, but institutional decisions remain decisions and difficult circumstances are an opportunity to bring core values into sharper focus. Universities have stood the test of centuries because they have always been rooted in something deeper than the economic and political storms blowing over them.

There is a well-known line, often attributed to Einstein but more reliably traced to sociologist W.B. Cameron:

Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.

It is a vital warning. In times of stress, universities can begin to value only what is easily measured: modules, student numbers, staff-student ratios, workload allocations, rankings, review scores and contribution margins. These matter. But they are not the sum total of a university’s value and worth.

Much of the important work universities do is slow, relational, civic and cumulative. It is built through trust, local knowledge and commitment. It sits awkwardly within workload models and is not easily attributable to one department, income stream or KPI. Yet this is often how universities fulfil their public and civic purpose.

This matters particularly for the Humanities and Social Sciences. These disciplines ask not just “what works?” but “for whom?”, “at what cost?”, “under what assumptions?” and “towards what kind of society?” They are central to good policy, democratic accountability and social mobility. These questions have become even more important in the AI revolution, which further increases the need to think about purpose, about what to do first and how to do it second.

They also matter for security. Government investment in defence-related higher education recognises the need for engineering, computing, cyber, robotics and autonomous systems. But if universities educate the next generation of defence specialists while weakening subjects that teach conflict resolution, ethics, diplomacy, history, languages and cooperation, then something has gone wrong. National security requires technical capability. But security in a broader sense – including policing and intelligence work – also requires knowledge of humanities. The judgement to prevent conflict and build cooperation remains human and not technological. Avoiding war is better than fighting one.

At the Centre for Social Mobility, our interdisciplinary work across data sciences, English literature, history, sociology and education sometimes sits beyond some metrics. Consider the Exam Access Project: a partnership between the University of Exeter, our local FE College, Exeter College, local authorities and AQA. The project enables young people who are out of school – often because of unmet needs, anxiety, sensory overload, off-rolling or other difficulties – to sit GCSE exams free of charge. Private exam entry can cost hundreds of pounds per subject. Until this project, there was no dedicated centre of this kind in Devon and Cornwall.

In its pilot year, the project supported 26 young people who were at serious risk of becoming NEET(not in education, employment or training). All 26 have now secured a next step into further study, training or an apprenticeship. We have had interest from over 30 local authorities to expand and replicate this pilot.

How should a university count that?

One could construct an individual and collective KPI: future earnings, reduced welfare costs, progression rates or regional skills benefits. Yet such measures still do not capture the human value of what has happened: a young person moving from exclusion to recognition; from a closed door to an exam desk; from a stalled pathway to choices. That is not easily priced. In any meaningful sense, it is priceless.

This kind of work is possible because regional universities are entwined with the places in which they sit. At regional institutions such as Exeter, staff live and work in the communities they serve, communities which are all too often neglected or misunderstood by metropolitan administrative centres. They raise children there, work with schools and colleges, serve on their PTAs and boards, support cultural institutions, contribute to civic and political life and encounter regional inequalities, transportation systems and water quality issues as lived realities. As a result, such universities have a special role in understanding the specific social landscapes of their regions and advocating for their needs. These responsibilities are not always visible in university metrics, but the loss of them is keenly felt whenever they are cut back or withdrawn.

University leadership is stewardship as well as financial management: holding together measurable outputs and immeasurable goods, institutional sustainability and public purpose. While it may seem prudent to cut while institutions still have manoeuvring space rather than when that is the only choice, there is not only danger that universities cut too much; it is that they cut the things they do not know how to value – and that cannot be easily restored once lost.

Universities need to count carefully. But they must also remember what cannot be counted.

title: Facing political attack and falling enrollment, colleges take the fight to … each other

The post Facing political attack and falling enrollment, colleges take the fight to … each other appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
It seemed like a win-win: a proposal to let community colleges in Illinois award bachelor’s degrees in certain subjects to rural residents and working adults who live beyond commuting distance of four-year universities.

The change would not only make things “easier and more affordable for students,” according to backers including Gov. JB Pritzker; it would increase the supply of workers with the skills employers need.

But four-year universities lined up against it. And a political ally, flanked by several of their presidents, was blunt about why: It would cut into their business.

“We’ll lose those students to the community college level,” Senate Majority Leader Kimberly Lightford pronounced.

Under attack from politicians, scorned by the public for their cost and facing unprecedented enrollment and financial problems, universities and colleges are responding by taking the fight to … each other.

At the same time that they’re lobbying against community college bachelor’s degrees, four-year universities are pursuing the exploding dual-enrollment and short-term workforce training markets community colleges have dominated.

The most selective among them are expanding their early decision programs to lock in more applicants and prevent them from enrolling elsewhere. Recruiters are poaching students from competing colleges, even after they’ve put down their deposits — something admissions officers once explicitly agreed to never do.

Public universities are dangling incentives to lure high school graduates from going to their own public university campuses in neighboring states. And private, nonprofit colleges are opening satellite branches in other schools’ backyards.

“This is the clash that occurs when you have declining populations overall and declining high school graduating classes,” said Davis Jenkins, senior research scholar at the Community College Research Center at Teachers College, Columbia University. (The Hechinger Report, which produced this story, is an independent unit of Teachers College.)

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Some of this intensifying competition could be a good thing for students and families, who are getting more choices as well as bigger discounts and other perks to enroll at colleges and universities that need to fill seats.

In many cases, however, “turf wars” and “mission creep” — as critics call this infighting — are heightening anxiety among consumers and preventing changes that could serve them.

“That was one of my biggest frustrations with the debate, because it felt like there wasn’t even a willingness to acknowledge a problem, and we have a problem in this state,” said Emily Shields, executive director of Community Colleges for Iowa, where lobbying by private four-year colleges blocked a plan to let community colleges in rural areas offer bachelor’s degrees.

“We have people in every region who would like to get a bachelor’s degree but can’t” because they live too far from four-year campuses and have families and jobs, Shields said.

More than 35 million people live beyond what the federal government defines as typical commuting distance from a public, four-year university, according to a study published by the Annenberg Institute at Brown University.

That’s among the reasons lawmakers in 24 states have passed laws allowing community colleges to offer bachelor’s degrees.

But momentum behind this approach has slowed, as four-year colleges worry it will siphon away some of their dwindling supply of students. Enrollment at universities and colleges nationwide already fell by nearly 2 million from 2010 to 2023 — the most recent period for which the figure is available — and the number of 18-year-olds, who make up most of their new customers, is projected to decline by 13 percent from this year until 2041.

Only about 76,000 students are enrolled in bachelor’s degree programs at community colleges nationwide, compared to 5.3 million at four-year colleges and universities. And research shows that most are 25 or older, and likely wouldn’t typically choose a four-year campus, and that adding bachelor’s degrees to community colleges does not significantly affect enrollment at their four-year public and private, nonprofit counterparts.

Related: More than a quarter of private colleges are at risk of closing, new projection shows

Yet in Iowa, private, four-year colleges argued that some would be forced to close if legislators let community colleges offer four-year degrees. The idea has also now stalled in Illinois, where more than a dozen community colleges are in areas where the nearest four-year university is too far away to commute.

An even bigger battleground in the fight for students is dual enrollment (also called dual credit, early college and concurrent enrollment), through which high school students take college-level courses for credit. Community colleges provide these courses to more than 70 percent of the high school students who take them, dominating a market that has quickly grown to 2.8 million students — so many that they now comprise more than a fifth of community college enrollment, overall, and the fastest-growing share of it.

This has not escaped the notice of four-year colleges and universities, which are adding their own dual-enrollment programs at an accelerating pace.

The number of four-year universities that have joined the National Alliance of Concurrent Enrollment Partnerships, or NACEP, which accredits these kinds of programs, went up by 36 schools between 2022 and last year — a 27 percent jump.

“To see that kind of increase really raised our eyebrows,” said Amy Williams, NACEP’s executive director.

The top reason institutions give for taking on this role, a NACEP survey found: as a recruiting tool.

While it may serve universities, this is not entirely helpful for students, NACEP warns. In 90 percent of high schools that offer dual enrollment, it found, more than one institution is now providing it. And in nearly 60 percent of those cases, two or more providers offer the same courses to students in the same high schools.

“Understandably, learners cite challenges navigating different enrollment deadlines, fee structures, degree pathways and transcript requests across institutions,” NACEP notes.

Related: Desperate for students, colleges resort to previously banned recruiting tactics

Four-year universities continue to expand their dual-enrollment offerings, however. Universities in Nevada, for instance, have been doing this, the state’s faculty association wrote, as “a means to mitigate the impacts of declining enrollment among their traditional students.” In the process, those faculty alleged, “quality and rigor are often trampled upon.”

Colorado lawmakers just passed legislation making it easier for four-year universities to provide more dual-enrollment courses in high schools in that state.

“Demographics are absolutely a factor” there, too, said John Albright, executive vice chancellor of the Colorado Community College System.

“There are fewer traditional-age students. Birthrates are declining. Institutions are responding to this,” Albright said. The question, he said, is whether adding more providers “expands opportunity and keeps pathways clear for students or creates a more fragmented system. We don’t know the answer to that.”

Four-year universities are targeting another traditional realm of, and growth area for, community colleges: short-term workforce training.

Enrollment in community college certificate programs is up 28 percent since the fall of 2021, a number likely to keep rising as students in these programs can now qualify for federal Pell Grants.

Seventy percent of four-year university and college presidents said they plan to add or expand short-term workforce training, according to a recent survey by Hanover Research and the industry news outlet Inside Higher Ed. It’s a strategic opportunity, the conservative think tank The Manhattan Institute has said — not only because such programs can attract students who would not enroll in degree programs, but also “to demonstrate concrete economic value and responsiveness to workforce needs” at a time of falling public faith in higher education.

Related: The biggest expansion of federal scholarship money in 50 years is at hand — and almost nobody is ready for it

But DeRionne Pollard, president and CEO of the American Association of Community Colleges, has some questions about the blurring of these boundaries.

“Is there a need that is not being met by the two-year institutions that have traditionally delivered dual-credit or workforce training in those communities?” Pollard asked. “What’s in the best interest of students? What’s in the best interest of the communities being served?”

Students and families, she said, “don’t need duplication or competition. They don’t need confusion. They need pathways” that will get them the educations they want, affordably and in a reasonable period of time — whatever kind of institution they attend.

“The future should be built on partnerships, not turf,” said Pollard.

It’s not just community colleges’ students four-year universities and colleges are going after. It’s each other’s.

Public universities in regions where the number of high school graduates has already started falling are offering lower tuition to graduates in bordering states and even farther-away but faster-growing places. California residents, for instance, can go to most State University of New York schools for the same price they would pay at a flagship public university in California.

Private, nonprofit four-year universities are opening satellite campuses in the territories of other institutions. Northeastern and Carnegie Mellon universities operate branches in the San Francisco Bay Area, for example, where Vanderbilt University will also open a campus next year.

The fiercest competition comes in the admissions process.

Selective schools that offer early decision — increasing the odds that applicants will get in, but barring them from considering any other college once they do — are relying more heavily on it, admitting larger proportions of their students that way, research from the advocacy organization Class Action finds. To encourage that commitment, some offer inducements such as priority housing, early move-in, parking privileges and meal plan upgrades.

For students admitted through the conventional process, meanwhile, recruiting now continues well past the day on which they put down their deposits — something previously banned by a provision in the code of ethics among admissions officers that was dropped in 2020 to settle a federal antitrust case.

Related: The number of 18-year-olds is about to drop sharply, packing a wallop for colleges — and the economy

“It became the Wild West after the antitrust settlement,” with colleges and universities poaching each other’s admitted students after the traditional May 1 deposit day, said Christy Pratt, former head of undergraduate admissions at the University of Notre Dame and a consultant at the executive search firm WittKieffer. Competition now drags on as late as September or October, when institutions close their books on the entering class.

That can mean lower prices for families, said David Attis, managing director of research advisory services at the enrollment management recruiting firm EAB. But it also “makes it much harder for students to plan and manage,” Attis said.

Nearly half of college and university applicants who were admitted from waiting lists said they were notified after May 1, according to a June survey by the college ratings platform Niche. That means most have already committed somewhere else, and have hard decisions to make, said Caroline Koppelman, founder and CEO of the private college admissions consulting firm The Koppelman Group.

“In general, the kids are more stressed out, and extending the admissions process doesn’t quell their anxiety,” Koppelman said.

To hedge their bets, students and families are increasingly putting down deposits at more than one school. Fourteen percent of students who entered college in the academic year just ended paid deposits to two or more universities or colleges, up from near-zero who did this in 2019, according to EAB. The wealthier the family, the more deposits it makes.

In some states, policymakers are stepping in to try to quash the wrangling over students. California legislators have proposed stripping the California State University System of authority it’s used repeatedly to stop community colleges from offering bachelor’s degrees, for example, as long as those degrees don’t duplicate programs available at nearby four-year universities.

In the end, said advocates, the best way for universities and colleges to vie for consumers is by giving them what they need.

“There are going to be these high-level squabbles over what are really small potatoes. What’s going to matter is that you offer value,” said Jenkins, the community college researcher.

“As far as trying to play nice in the sandbox,” added Albright, in Colorado, “everyone has a shared interest in trying to be responsive to students.”

title: AAUP Denounces Politician, Donor ‘Extortion’ of Universities
summary:
AAUP Denounces Politician, Donor ‘Extortion’ of Universities
Ryan Quinn Thu, 07/23/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
Donors, state politicians and Trump administration officials are extorting universities to get them to give up their autonomy, the American Association of University Professors says.

“The federal government has used the threat of withholding billions of dollars in research funding, not to enforce civil rights law, but to demand sweeping changes to institutional governance, hiring, curriculum and campus policies,” AAUP President Todd Wolfson said Wednesday at a news conference.

The AAUP—the 111-year-old professional organization that wrote seminal definitions of academic freedom and tenure, and a left-leaning faculty union—released a new report Wednesday titled “Extorted Compliance: A Threat to Institutional Autonomy, Academic Freedom, and Shared Governance.” It recounts what it calls an attack on higher ed and faculty accelerating over the past decade as part of “a far-reaching effort spearheaded by forces on the political right to remake not only higher education but the entire political landscape, to some extent as part of a broader international antidemocratic movement.”

The report especially focuses on the second Trump administration’s actions, including how it pressured Columbia University to make concessions through cutting its research funding and its proposed “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education.” But Wolfson said that “if any administration, Republican or Democratic, can use financial leverage to compel universities to surrender their independence,” then institutional autonomy, academic freedom and shared governance become conditional.

Rana Jaleel, chair of the AAUP’s Committee A on Academic Freedom and Tenure, said, “In aggregate, these are not good-faith attempts to improve how universities function,” but instead efforts to “coerce higher education into functioning as an ideological arm of the state.”

“What to research, what to teach [and] how to ensure that all—and not just some—of the public is served by higher education would no longer, in their vision, be determined by people who have spent their lives learning and training to address these issues,” Jaleel said. “Instead, those people are being pushed aside so that politicians can tell us what to do.”

The White House didn’t respond to requests for comment.

title: Getting Real About Institutional Finances
summary:
Getting Real About Institutional Finances
sara.custer@in… Thu, 07/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

At NACUBO’s annual meeting, a keynote speaker’s exercise in vulnerability set the tone for conversations about money—and why higher ed’s financial future depends on honesty, not just numbers.

Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
I avoid group activities at higher ed conferences like parasite-infected lettuce. They’re too personal. I don’t do let’s-be-vulnerable-with-strangers. And being a journalist, it can feel like I’m an interloper in higher ed’s tight-knit professional communities. I have no relatable work experiences to share.

But this week at the National Association of College and University Business Officers’ annual meeting, keynote speaker Suneel Gupta, an author and host of Amazon Prime’s Business Class, tricked me into sharing. Before I could slip out the back, Gupta had us pull the note cards from under our chairs and write down our biggest worry in life, anonymously. Then, I was among the 1,600 attendees walking the enormous hall swapping card after card and writing “+1” on the back if we’d ever felt the same thing.

I learned that someone’s middle child was probably going to jail and they are draining their retirement fund to pay the legal fees. Another person was terrified by the world her unborn child is coming into. I read that someone’s father recently died and without his guidance they felt adrift. Several people were worried about excelling in their careers and still being able to show up for their family. A scary number of marriages were in trouble.

This was heavy stuff for 9:00 a.m. on a Sunday morning in the cavernous Anaheim Convention Center. But it was effective in communicating Gupta’s message to the chief financial officers leading the country’s higher ed institutions: Never worry alone. He reminded them that beneath their numbers, data and meetings, they are impacting people’s lives, even in the smallest ways.

Despite my queasiness over an exercise in vulnerability and honesty, I realized that at a time when higher ed institutions are facing existential financial worries, there was no better way to kick off a meeting of the people in charge of the money. Because no matter how dire a budget looks, the real challenge to overcome is always people.

That same idea—don’t worry alone—surfaced in sessions over the course of the three-day event. Honest and clear communication among CFOs, presidents and the board is mission-critical, yet so many colleges struggle with it. Leslie Brunelli, the executive vice president for finance and administration and chief financial officer at Washington State University, described the “magical thinking” at this level of governance: “Regents think that if we just explain to faculty the situation, they’ll be OK with us cutting their program,” she said. It’s not that the board doesn’t understand finances; they just don’t understand higher ed.

Gerald Hector, executive vice president and chief financial officer at Morehouse School of Medicine, said CFOs have to be storytellers that turn “accountant-ese” into something institutional leaders can understand. “Make it as basic as possible without overwhelming them,” he said, adding that data is key. “Present the facts in a way that is indisputable. Use trends and benchmarking to take the emotions out of it.”

In other sessions, CFOs shared their concerns about the rising cost of athletics. They encouraged each other to be honest with campus leaders about deferred maintenance and transparent in their endowment reports to donors.

Academic program costs are another place where campus culture makes honest communication about money hard. And still, according to Inside Higher Ed’s 2026 Survey of College and University Business Officers, academic program restructuring is the most important structural change institutions need to make in the next three years to remain financially viable. Yet, just 13 percent of CBOs say their institution understands per-student program and activity costs very well. Responding to that figure in a session at the event, Laura De Veau, visiting assistant professor in education leadership and higher education at Boston College, said, “That’s bananas!” She added, “The costs have to match what we’re bringing in.”

Money is always about more than what’s in the bank. Higher ed finances are no different. Boards are full of alumni with emotional ties to a decrepit residence hall that should be razed. Deans are territorial over their budgets. Faculty and staff often don’t understand that costs are rising faster than state appropriations. But with greater honesty and vulnerability from everyone on campus about the true state of an institution’s finances, leaders will be better placed to make the tough decisions that could shore up their institutions’ future.

‘I am acutely conscious,” said Andy Burnham outside 10 Downing Street on Monday, “that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street.” It was good to hear him say it because, beneath all the cabinet gossip and rune-reading, there is a feeling of terror about the immediate future and also about ourselves, the electorate. Is this who we are now? Wildly enthusiastic one minute, seething the next; as passionate about the change we want as we are convinced that those who promise it are incapable of enacting it?

It is perhaps not surprising that Anton Jäger’s recent book, Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization without Political Consequences, is being read by Labour watchers and leftwing thinkers. As the New York Times wrote, it’s “among the best and most dazzling efforts to model the political present in all its maddening strangeness”. Still, I think Jäger was surprised to have his honeymoon interrupted so I could interview him about it. Life comes at everyone quite fast in a hyperpolitical age.

Jäger, 32, raised in Brussels by parents who work in the arts (“bohemian class?” I ask, and he says carefully that they are boho “adjacent”), educated at the University of Essex, then Cambridge, is now a lecturer in the history of political thought and theory at University College, Oxford. He has an intense, angular face and a calm, almost self-effacing manner. His philosophical reference points are Deleuze and Guattari, Mouffe and Laclau, but asked to situate himself in the firmament of the European left, he says simply: “Even with all the baggage and connotations, I still think the easiest thing is to call myself a Marxist.”

His thinking runs as follows (don’t get hung up on the dates, though some, like 1989, are non-negotiable). The years 1914 to 1989 mark the age of mass politics, when politicisation was high and institutionalisation was also high – so people engaged with politics electorally and on the streets. They were joiners – of political parties, unions, congregations, working men’s clubs, reading groups; they participated in multiple interlacing institutions. Not by coincidence, this was also a time when political struggle resulted in concrete gains. Then, 1989 to the financial crash in 2008 (the years often called the “long 90s”) was the age of post-politics, when institutionalisation was low (we emphatically did not join clubs then, we went to clubs), and politicisation was through the floor. It was a time when technocrats took care of business while everyone else went to a rave, and we said history was over. From the crash through to about 2020 (sometimes earlier, this boundary is the most fluid) was the age of anti-politics – a resurgent Tea Party in the US, Beppe Grillo and anti-establishment protests in Italy, the Arab spring, the Occupy movement. Politicisation in this period came back with a vengeance, and even while institutionalisation hasn’t recovered, these movements still have institutional ambitions. Protest movements in Spain and Greece bore political parties, Podemos and Syriza; protest candidates in the US, France and the UK, had their eyes on retaking traditional parties from which the revolutionary intent had long been stripped away.

Hyperpolitics is what came next: intense politicisation, with neither institutional roots nor ambitions. “On the surface,” Jäger writes, “the Black Lives Matter protests would seem to have little in common with the mob that stormed the Capitol in January 2021. Morally, they are worlds apart … Organisationally, however, these movements exhibit a striking set of similarities: fleeting in duration, they maintain no membership rolls and struggle to impose any real discipline on their adherents.” As a consequence, everything explodes and nothing changes; movements surge suddenly forward and yet no territory is taken. He quotes political theorist Paolo Gerbaudo’s evocative phrase “bodies without organs”. Modern political movements, he writes, are “concentrated and muscular, yet without an internal metabolism”.

He found this pattern across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and he only stopped there, he says, because “I don’t have the linguistic and cultural reach to fully tell this story globally”. His descriptions are powerful. He writes of climate strikers and anti-lockdown demonstrators alike as “a myriad animated by brief, potent stimuli, stirred to action by charismatic influencers and digital demagogues”. And that, you have to admit, is exactly what it looks like.

These four eras – mass politics, post-politics, antipolitics and hyperpolitics – “are not just concepts,” Jäger says, “they have some empirical data behind them. ‘How institutionalised is society?’ is basically a question of, how does civil society look? How are membership organisations looking? What are the affiliations, what are the types of bonds that people have? That’s not very difficult to quantify. You can look at union membership, you can look at church attendance, you can look at less overtly political forms of belonging. The political axis is more difficult to measure, but not impossible – namely, how many people attend elections, how many people strike, how many people engage in political violence, how many people engage in political communication, write letters to editors or now post online?”

He argues that the height of mass politics was between the wars. To illustrate this in the book, he lists all the civic organisations during the Great Depression in the small Rhenish hamlet of Marienthal – they spanned all human activity, from work to thought to rabbit-breeding. I won’t list them all here but there were many. Considering the effect these organisations might have on the collective psyche, Jäger considers the history of his own family: “On the Flemish side, this meant that the Christian Democratic or the Catholic party was not just a party that said how you were to vote, or which union you joined, but also had a very strong say in what happened in the bedroom. It was a total doctrine, not something that purely applied to your political deportment.” There was little boundary between public and private, and no such thing as a political identity without a membership card. It was personally quite constraining, but it got shit done. (Sidebar, I’ve seen a nascent institutionalised-politics like this, in Manchester, in 2019; the local Momentum group was campaigning for Jeremy Corbyn, but it also had a running club, a knitting group and a book group. I was overcome by the sense of seeing a trade union movement reborn. Needless to say, Corbyn did not win that election. Institution-building can’t be done on the fly.)

The destruction of political organisations was “not monocausal”, Jäger says, though in the book he puts it squarely on the shoulders of the union busting by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan. People lost faith in organisations because the crunchy bit of their leverage – the bit where you get what you want by withdrawing your labour, the bit before all-out war – was taken away. Unions were defanged and workers impoverished, and many ultimately saw their industries collapse in the process.

Jäger says there were also cultural and generational shifts over decades – people in the 60s and 70s seeking a different relationship with collective institutions, for example, and looking instead for emancipation and equality – so it takes a while for the picture to cohere, and Communist parties remained tenacious through the 1980s in Italy, for instance. “In 1989, suddenly it’s as if there’s a day and night difference,” he says. With the fall of the Berlin Wall, the end of the cold war, he says: “Suddenly everyone deserves to party.”

It is a strange sensation to have the 90s narrated back to you by someone who was born in 1994, but it is mainly unsettling because it is so accurate. Tony Blair did describe globalisation as a process as inexorable as the weather, and that is also how neoliberals described the economy – a thing that happened to you. “This is the ambiguity of the post-politics of the 90s,” Jäger says. “Politics is no longer something that you see as effecting large-scale social change, and the forms of liberty that are available to you are now more private, more intimate, more individual. At the same time, the idea that you can collectively bundle together with other individuals and change society starts to appear very, very remote.”

There was also a lot of beauty to that time, which he describes through the photography of Wolfgang Tillmans and the novels of Annie Ernaux and Michel Houellebecq. We were obsessed with Houellebecq in the 90s, but we will have to talk about why, and the direction his novels took, and whether we will ever again live in a world whose best cultural artefact is the novel, another time. “The fact that Tillmans as a gay man is able to express and experience the rave culture of the 90s and 00s as a new form of collectivity that wasn’t available to him in the 70s and 80s, I don’t think we should deny the liberatory value of this. It very clearly is the case that there are individuals who did not feel at home in the families, or the communities or the neighbourhoods in which they grew up, in which they finally find a kind of new community that is much less demanding and is less exigent than what they had before. The ambiguity is, of course, that it also implies a profound disenchantment and cynicism around what politics can do.” That’s politics with a capital P – you might see a community animated about an issue, but with no faith in parliamentary channels.

There is a critical and rarely mentioned adjunct to the neoliberal destruction of institutions and the post and antipolitics that came afterwards, which is that it didn’t only come for the left. “Thatcher basically did a controlled demolition of popular Conservatism,” Jäger says, “and replaced much of this with PR spin, and also a lot of private funding, because the idea was: ‘We can get rid of our mass party because we’re in control of the media, we can win elections with that.’” The right today, he says, is just as inconsequential as the left, and for exactly the same reason, that it’s hyper but not formally organised. “The people who go on marches subscribe to the same podcast, might follow the same pages on Instagram, might be on the same Telegram channels, but they don’t have an organisational history they shared before they entered the march. This is different even to the BNP, where marchers had a shared history in football hooliganism, and the National Front. That shared subculture is no longer there.”

He says this is clear with Reform UK, “which is so heavily leader-dependent. The entire movement is at risk with this scandal of the crypto-billionaire, because there’s no party infrastructure. There is just Nigel and a smartphone and then a couple of private donors.” To me, this fails to take into account that the right is different to the left: they have more money. “Maybe I understated the availability of private funding,” he says mildly. “The fact that we can even talk of a trillionaire, such as Elon Musk, means there’s a complete secession of that individual from what we could even call society. That is a variable in explaining why hyperpolitics on the right thrives and why hyperpolitics on the left has found it much more difficult to achieve tangible results.” They are not more organised or more ideologically coherent or more strategic; they are just better funded – which puts quite a lot on the shoulders of capital itself as the overarching organising principle of global politics. Money might not be the only thing talking, but it’s the only thing getting what it wants.

The more immediately controversial proposition of the book, though, is that what we are watching in Trump’s US is not fascism, because the right only travels to that extreme in the face of a direct threat of organised socialism. “The left is doing itself too many favours by considering its opponents fascists,” he says. “You’re overestimating your strength. The contemporary far right is more a function of the crisis of liberalism than it is a function of the strength of the left.” What we’re looking at instead, with Trump, is “Bonapartism” says Jäger. He writes that Trump, and everyone else who has ever got ahead by championing the “left behind”, isn’t representing a strong mass movement or class, but, like Napoleon, relying on “the largely passive support of impoverished peasants … not a collective but ‘formed by the simple addition of isomorphous magnitudes, much as potatoes in a sack form a sack of potatoes’.” (That bit about potatoes is from Karl Marx’s The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte.) We skirmish a little about the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a standing army that looks extremely fascist, until Jäger concludes: “The spectrum from fascism to Bonapartism can flip into something more radical. At the same time, I’m still more struck by the differences than the similarities with these 20th-century phenomena.”

Neal Lawson, guru of Manchesterism and an Anton Jäger fan, lays these arguments over the predicament of our new prime minister. “It isn’t just lack of money Burnham has to contend with but the absence of secure political footings. Temporary hyper-political swarms have taken the place of substantial and secure alliances. He must find a way to surf these volatile waves or be another victim of them.” But we, the volatile waves, also have to figure out how to re-engage with institutions and build new ones, and is that possible? Jäger pauses, dispiritingly, like a mechanic who is about to give you bad news about your fanbelt. “This is an interesting and scary question. We do live in a society in which the incentives for leaving rather than entering organisations are much higher. Recent experience, whether joining a party or joining a union, often militates against the idea that there’s any sense in collective action, and the rational response is helplessness. And yet, repoliticisation is good. Hyperpolitics has increased people’s consciousness of the fact that politics matters.”

title: Beyond paper leaks, the question of trust and institutional integrity
summary: The uniqueness of the present agitation lies in one of the most powerful aspirations in contemporary India: the belief that education and competitive examinations provide a pathway to social and economic mobility.
full_text:
Every major protest, at some point, becomes a battle of narratives. The student movement over NEET and recurring examination paper leaks has now reached that stage.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi reached out to the youth and their parents, promising that his government would bring a law to stringently deal with paper leaks, after announcing the setting up of fast-track courts.

The announcement came less than 24 hours after Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi framed the issue as one of “police brutality” against students and declared that “they are our future, not terrorists”.

The competing responses underscored how the political contest has shifted beyond the immediate issue of exam irregularities to a larger battle over public perception.

The BJP’s wider political ecosystem, aided by sections of the media, has sought to portray the protesters as anti-national or as being backed by vested interests seeking to spread anarchy. Such narratives have proved to be politically effective in the past. This time, however, they appear to have found limited resonance beyond the party’s core support base.

The uniqueness of the present agitation lies in one of the most powerful aspirations in contemporary India: the belief that education and competitive examinations provide a pathway to social and economic mobility.

Every leaked examination paper undermines not just a recruitment process but the social contract that hard work and merit will ultimately be rewarded. For thousands of families, preparing for competitive examinations is not merely an academic exercise but a years-long investment involving financial sacrifice, emotional strain and the hope of economic security. Any perception that the system is compromised therefore strikes at something far deeper than administrative failure.

Equally significant is the age profile of the protesters. The faces of this movement are not seasoned political activists or hardened trade unionists but students in their late teens and twenties — the very demographic that has been central to the BJP’s political messaging around aspiration, opportunity and a “New India”.

Images of police dragging young aspirants carrying the national flag and examination identity cards evoke a very different public response from confrontations involving organised political groups. The optics are difficult for any government. Parents who may disagree with the Opposition’s politics can still identify with the anxieties of students preparing for examinations. And that explains why the Opposition’s messaging has resonated beyond its traditional political constituency.

And that is also why perhaps Prime Minister made an appeal close to midnight on Thursday (July 23, 2026).

The students’ agitation is unlike any of the major protests that the Narendra Modi government has confronted over the past 12 years. The anti-CAA movement quickly acquired communal and constitutional dimensions. The farmers’ agitation, despite its national resonance, remained concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and parts of western Uttar Pradesh. The wrestlers’ protest revolved around allegations against a powerful individual.

The current movement is different because competitive examinations cut across caste, religion, language and region. Every cancelled or compromised examination reinforces the fear that success not only depends on merit but also on the institutional integrity.

Ironically, the government’s own political slogan — aapda mein avsar (opportunity in adversity) — offers a possible way out of the crisis. Over the past decade, the Modi government has cultivated an image of decisiveness and centralised authority. While that has projected strength, it has also created the perception that the government is reluctant to acknowledge institutional failures or undertake course correction.

By engaging directly with students, fixing accountability for paper leaks, strengthening examination systems and demonstrating institutional transparency, the government can show that decisiveness and responsiveness are not mutually exclusive. Such an approach would also reinforce the message that acknowledging failures is not a sign of political weakness but of institutional confidence.

While it is true that the education sector is always a long term ideological and political project of any party in power, any government that jeopardises the future of students will have to pay a political price.

Democracies derive legitimacy not only from electoral victories alone but also from their ability to listen, acknowledge mistakes and rebuild trust. The government’s response to this movement will therefore be judged not merely by whether it could hold an examination successfully, but by whether it restores confidence among a generation whose faith has been shaken by the course of events.

title: From exam leaks to a national movement: Inside the protests reshaping India’s education debate
summary:
What began as outrage over the alleged NEET paper leak has evolved into a nationwide student protest movement. Reporting from Mumbai, The PIE explores why students say the crisis has become about far more than one examination or one minister.

The post From exam leaks to a national movement: Inside the protests reshaping India’s education debate appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
“Dharmendra Pradhan istifa do.” (“Dharmendra Pradhan, resign.”)

The chant rolled across Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on Wednesday evening as thousands of students, graduates, parents, job seekers and supporters gathered around one of the city’s most recognisable public spaces.

For hours, demonstrators occupied the roads surrounding the historic ground, long associated with political rallies and public movements.

From balconies overlooking the procession, residents watched the march unfold. Some applauded as protesters passed below, while others filmed the demonstration from their homes.

The immediate demand was clear: the resignation of union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The protests trace their origins to the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET-UG), India’s nationwide entrance examination for undergraduate medical and dental programs.

More than 2.2 million candidates sat this year’s examination before authorities cancelled it following allegations that the question paper had been leaked, forcing students to sit an unprecedented nationwide re-examination weeks later.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which is probing the alleged leak, has arrested 13 people and says it has uncovered what investigators describe as a multi-state network involving individuals linked to the examination process, coaching teachers and intermediaries.

According to the agency, questions from the Physics, Chemistry and Biology papers were allegedly circulated to students before the examination in exchange for money, with searches conducted across dozens of locations continuing as investigators prepare to file a chargesheet.

The controversy has also been accompanied by reports of dozens of NEET-linked student suicides this year, transforming what began as an examination scandal into a broader debate about the psychological toll of India’s intensely competitive entrance examination system.

For many protesters, the deaths have become as central to the movement as the alleged paper leak itself.

“The government has for years shown apathy towards us and our rights,” one protester told The PIE News. “We believe the education system in this country needs thorough reform, and people who fail to take accountability should resign.”

The crowd reflected that broader frustration.

Medical aspirants marched alongside university students, recent graduates, unemployed youths, parents and working professionals. Many of those attending appeared to be in their late teens and 20s.

Yet despite the palpable anger, the demonstration remained notably disciplined.

Volunteers directed traffic at busy junctions, reminded demonstrators not to use abusive language and encouraged participants to avoid disrupting commuters and local residents. Throughout the evening, organisers moved through the crowd checking on participants and helped manage the march.

At the same time, there was an unmistakable sense of caution.

Police maintained a visible presence around Shivaji Park while vehicles used to transport detainees repeatedly made their way around the protest route. Whenever they appeared, warnings spread quickly through the gathering. Protesters alerted one another, with some moving between locations in groups as a precaution against possible detentions.

The scenes unfolding in Mumbai reflected a movement that has rapidly expanded across India.

Initially fuelled by outrage over the NEET controversy, the demonstrations have evolved into broader calls for accountability and education reform, with protests taking place in several cities. One of the biggest ones is happening in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar site.

If a failed and incompetent minister is being considered more important than these crores of students, then remember: no one in India will vote for you in the elections

Abhijit Dipke, Cockroach Janata Party

Much of that momentum has been channelled through a newly formed youth-led organisation. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical movement whose name parodies the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Back at Shivaji Park, those wider national developments were reflected in both the slogans adorning placards and the overall mood.

Frustration was directed not only at Pradhan but also at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and what protesters repeatedly referred to as the “Godi media”—a pejorative term used by critics to describe sections of India’s mainstream media they believe have become overly sympathetic to the BJP.

The movement has also drawn national attention through engineer and activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose hunger strike became one of its defining symbols. After being admitted to hospital, Wangchuk said he was willing to end his fast if the government guaranteed that students participating in the demonstrations would not face retaliatory action.

As protests continued across Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and elsewhere, Modi made his first public intervention since the demonstrations escalated, announcing that the government would establish fast-track courts to ensure “swift and stringent punishment” in paper leak cases.

“Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth,” Modi wrote on X, adding that those responsible for harming students’ futures “will not be spared.”

Protest organisers, however, argue that criminal prosecutions alone cannot resolve what they see as deeper structural problems within India’s examination system.

CJP founding president Abhijeet Dipke urged Modi to remove Pradhan from office, warning that public anger could eventually extend to the prime minister himself.

“Modi ji, I once again request you to accept Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. Otherwise, the issue will not remain limited to Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation alone; it will come for your resignation also,” Dipke said.

“An incompetent and failed minister cannot be more important than the crores of students in this country. If a failed and incompetent minister is being considered more important than these crores of students, then remember: no one in India will vote for you in the elections.”

By late evening, the crowd at Shivaji Park had begun to thin, but thousands had already remained there for hours.

Police vehicles continued to make their rounds. Protesters continued warning one another to stay together while volunteers guided people safely through the surrounding streets.

What had begun as outrage over a leaked entrance examination had, for many gathered in Mumbai, become something far broader: a demand to restore confidence in an education system they believed had failed them.

“If we don’t speak up now,” one student said, “it won’t just be our generation. Future generations will continue going through the same education system, one that creates psychological pressure instead of encouraging genuine, care-driven learning.”

title: Sunway University awards honorary master’s degree to Malaysian popstar Siti Nurhaliza
