title: UK unis join forces to offer study pathways for visa brake students
summary:
Nine UK universities are working alongside the NGO Mosaik Education to provide remote postgraduate study opportunities to international students from countries subject to a strict study visa pause.

The post UK unis join forces to offer study pathways for visa brake students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The universities have committed places through the Mosaik Scholarship, a new initiative providing alternative pathways to UK postgraduate education for students affected by the Home Office’s “visa brake” introduced in March.

It followed rising concerns over asylum claims made by international students, with the government claiming that students from Myanmar, Cameroon, Sudan and Afghanistan were proportionally the worst culprits and pausing study visa applications from these nations.

The policy prevented students from the four countries from accessing UK campus-based scholarships, including the Chevening program, through which around 50 students from these communities previously accessed postgraduate study each year.

So far, 19 funded places have been secured through commitments from King’s College London, the University of London, the University of Leicester, the University of Northampton, the University of St Andrews, Cardiff University, Birkbeck, University of London, the University of Salford and Aberystwyth University, in partnership with Higher Ed Partners UK.

All programs will be delivered through online or transnational education (TNE) routes, currently the only available pathways for new students from the affected countries to gain a UK degree.

The initiative has been coordinated through the Global Response Platform, a sector-wide collaboration led by Mosaik Education that connects UK universities with humanitarian networks supporting displaced and crisis-affected students.

Through the platform, universities receive support identifying and selecting students, as well as coordinating with partners in affected regions, including UNHCR India, Prospect Burma and Open Dreams in Cameroon.

Further university commitments are expected later in 2026, with the initiative aiming to support around 50 students overall.

Ben Webster, CEO of Mosaik Education, said the collaboration demonstrated how the sector could respond collectively when traditional routes to education were disrupted.

“For students in Afghanistan, Myanmar, Sudan and Cameroon, a UK scholarship was one of very few viable ways to continue an education that conflict had already disrupted once,” he said.

“The visa brake closed this route for them. With UK universities teaching over 650,000 students outside the UK, the infrastructure to reach these students has always been there. What was missing was a way for the sector to act on it together.”

With UK universities teaching over 650,000 students outside the UK, the infrastructure to reach these students has always been there. What was missing was a way for the sector to act on it together

Ben Webster, Mosaik Education

Professor Sally Wheeler, vice-chancellor of Birkbeck, University of London, said: the institution was “proud” to offer new routes to students who would otherwise not get access to UK higher education.

The initiative also highlights the growing role of online and TNE in expanding access to UK higher education for students unable to relocate.

Professor Phil Allmendinger, pro vice-chancellor (education) at the University of London, said: “The University of London is proud to support the Mosaik Scholarship and to stand alongside partner institutions in ensuring that talented students affected by conflict, displacement and restrictions on mobility are not excluded from higher education.”

Jo Purves, pro vice-chancellor partnerships and global engagement at the University of Salford, added that the scheme reflected the university’s commitment to ensuring students were not prevented from accessing education because of their location.

“As a University of Sanctuary with a strong history of offering distance learning and transnational education, Salford looks forward to welcoming these students into the global academic community,” she said.

Mosaik Education is now calling on additional UK universities with online or TNE provision to join the initiative and commit further places.

title: English universities face “unstable hybrid” future, warns HEPI report
summary:
English higher education is heading towards an “unstable hybrid” future as financial pressures intensify faster than expected, according to a new report from the Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI).

The post English universities face “unstable hybrid” future, warns HEPI report appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
English higher education is heading towards an “unstable hybrid” future as financial pressures intensify faster than expected, according to a new report from the Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI).

The report, New Choices: Revisiting Futures for Higher Education in England, written by Chris Husbands, warns that the sector is now moving towards a combination of decline, concentrated research activity and stalled regional reform, without a clear strategy to manage the changes.

The paper follows Husbands’ 2024 report, Four Futures, which outlined four possible scenarios for how universities could respond to growing financial pressures. Two years later, he argues that the challenges identified have arrived sooner than anticipated and have been compounded by wider disruption.

“Simply increasing income is no longer a viable strategy for institutions and simply hoping the market sorts itself out is no longer a viable strategy for government,” said Husbands.

“What the sector needs now is a combination of government activism and institutional courage,” he added.

The report highlights mounting financial pressures across English higher education, including forecasts from the Office for Students that 45% of providers will be in deficit in 2025/26, with 45 institutions holding fewer than 30 days of liquidity.

It also points to rising restructuring costs, with sector-wide severance spending increasing by 71% year-on-year to £303 million, while the academic workforce contracted for the first time in more than a decade.

The increase in the undergraduate tuition fee cap to £9,790 in 2025 has delivered only limited financial relief, the report argues, with a sector-wide net gain of around £18m after increased employer National Insurance costs are taken into account.

Alongside financial pressures, Husbands identifies other forces impacting universities, including declining public confidence in the value and purpose of higher education.

The report notes that the proportion of people in Britain who believe a degree is not worth the time and money has increased from 14% in 2005 to 34% today.

“In the long run, the sector’s legitimacy depends on demonstrating public value, either through the strength of its core teaching and research or through universities’ wider contributions,” said Husbands in the report.

“Questions of public value have become more pressing because the sector’s claims to success appear weaker in both areas: in teaching, because perceived graduate economic returns have declined; and in wider impact, because rising university participation has coincided with stalled productivity and economic growth.”

Husbands argues that the current direction of travel is “less stable than any of the original scenarios” set out in Four Futures.

Looking ahead, Husbands outlines a possible future structure for English higher education, with a smaller number of globally competitive research universities, a larger group of regionally focused institutions, more connected local universities working with private providers, and specialist institutions built around distinctive disciplines or teaching models.

He calls on universities to reconsider their operating models, partnerships and roles within their communities.

The report also urges government to provide greater policy clarity on areas including teaching funding, the Lifelong Learning Entitlement, the relationship between international student recruitment and immigration policy, research funding, regulation and a framework for managed mergers and institutional exits.

Speaking to The PIE News, a spokesperson for Universities UK responded to the concerns laid out in the report.

A university education doesn’t just benefit the individual: if we want our country to grow, we need more graduates entering the labour market. Sustaining that depends on universities being properly funded

Universities UK

“A university education doesn’t just benefit the individual: if we want our country to grow, we need more graduates entering the labour market. Sustaining that depends on universities being properly funded,” they said.

“Universities are one of this country’s greatest assets, driving economic growth in every part of the UK and helping local communities thrive. Yet they are under real financial pressure.

“Tuition fees are now worth only two thirds of what they were in 2012, because for years universities were not allowed to increase them in line with inflation. The sector is tackling this head on, finding back office savings and increasingly working together to become more efficient.”

However, the advocacy organisation warned that universities “cannot close the gap alone”.

title: Each Student Has a Different Door: What I Learned About Learning Styles from Andrew Cohen — and from My Own Students
summary:
After attending a summer workshop on learning strategies led by Professor Andrew Cohen, I returned to my Spanish classrooms at Northwestern University with a simple question: What would happen if my students became aware of how they learned?  To explore this, I introduced an anonymous learning strategies survey that I had adapted from one I had […]

The post Each Student Has a Different Door: What I Learned About Learning Styles from Andrew Cohen — and from My Own Students appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
After attending a summer workshop on learning strategies led by Professor Andrew Cohen, I returned to my Spanish classrooms at Northwestern University with a simple question: What would happen if my students became aware of how they learned?

To explore this, I introduced an anonymous learning strategies survey that I had adapted from one I had learned during the workshop (https://tinyurl.com/2j39ka6m). I explained that their honest responses would help me support their learning and asked them to complete it at home so they could reflect honestly. The next day, to ensure anonymity, I asked students to place their completed surveys into an envelope and stepped out of the room while they submitted them. This small gesture encouraged openness and trust.

The survey asked students to reflect on their listening, vocabulary, speaking, reading, and writing. The goal was not to evaluate them, but to help them understand their own learning.

Their responses transformed my teaching. For the first time, I saw the diversity of learning strategies in my classroom. Some relied on memorization, even when it was ineffective. Others described strategies such as listening to music, visualizing words, or repeating phrases aloud. Several students said they had never been asked to reflect on how they learned. They began to realize their difficulties did not reflect lack of ability, but a mismatch between how they studied and how they learned best.

Based on what I learned, I made small but meaningful changes, encouraging students to use visual flashcards, personal writing, music, and oral repetition to support their learning.

The classroom environment also shifted. Students became more confident and patient with themselves and others. Learning was no longer an isolated struggle, but a shared process.

Looking back, this survey produced three important outcomes: greater metacognitive awareness, more responsive instruction, and increased learner autonomy.

Around this time, I encountered the Integrated Performance Assessment (IPA) model developed by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL), which organizes language learning into interpretive, interpersonal, and presentational modes. This framework was important because it gave structure to what I had begun to see: language learning happens through multiple forms of engagement, and each student enters through a different door.

In the end, my students were not only learning Spanish. They were teaching me how learning happens.

Practical Takeaway: Invite Students to Reflect on Their Learning

Instructors can build on a learning strategies survey by:

Asking students to discuss which strategies work best for them

Encouraging students to experiment with new approaches

Designing activities that include listening, speaking, reading, and writing

Normalizing the idea that learners use different pathways

These conversations help students become more confident, independent, and engaged.

When Students Teach the Teacher

As I read my students’ surveys, I began to realize that many had never been asked how they learned. They had been graded and corrected but rarely invited to reflect on their learning processes.

Their answers were revealing. One student needed repetition. Another relied on writing by hand. Another used visualization and personal associations. Their challenges were not about effort, but alignment between teaching and learning.

And this realization changed how I taught—and how I listened. I began paying closer attention to how students approached learning. Their reflections helped me see patterns I had previously overlooked and reminded me that effective teaching begins with understanding the learner.

I introduced activities that allowed multiple entry points into the language, including music, personal writing, and oral practice. Students became more confident and willing to experiment. They began to see that there was not one correct way to learn.

In the same time, the IPA framework helped guide these instructional choices. Its emphasis on interpretive, interpersonal, and presentational communication allowed me to design activities that supported the diverse learning processes already present in my classroom. Instead of expecting all students to learn in the same way, I could help each of them engage with the language more effectively.

My students were not only learning Spanish. They were teaching me how to teach.

Practical Takeaway: Align Instruction with How Students Learn

Instructors can build on student strategy awareness by:

Asking students to share which learning techniques help them most

Offering options for practice, such as visual, written, and oral activities

Encouraging students to experiment and reflect on what works

Adjusting instruction based on student feedback

When instruction aligns with how students learn, engagement and confidence increase.

Listening to My Students: What the Survey Revealed

One of the most revealing parts of the survey was not only how students learned, but why they were learning Spanish.

Their motivations were deeply personal. Some wanted to travel or advance professionally. Others wanted to communicate with people they loved. I still remember the laughter when one student said, “My girlfriend is from Colombia. I need to speak with her family.” Another said simply, “My boyfriend is from Spain. I don’t want translation to be part of our relationship.” In that moment, language was not an assignment. It was a bridge.

The survey also helped students recognize their strengths. Many discovered they were visual learners and began using images and flashcards. Others relied on repetition, writing, or meaningful communication. As students became more aware of how they learned, their confidence grew.

Years later, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I carried this lesson into a different classroom while I volunteered to teach Hebrew on Zoom to students across Latin America and the United States. Many were learning Hebrew as part of a personal journey of identity and connection.

Remembering my earlier experience, I invited them to reflect on how they learned. Their responses were familiar, but my role had changed. I was no longer discovering their differences for the first time. I was listening to them intentionally.

In the end, I learned something essential: Teaching begins with listening.

And the question that continues to guide me is simple: How can we help students discover how they learn?

Practical Takeaways for Instructors

Instructors can apply this approach by:

Asking students how they learn

Using anonymous surveys or reflective discussions

Offering multiple ways to practice and engage

Encouraging students to experiment with strategies

Even small conversations about learning can transform student confidence and engagement.

Rifka Epstein is a language educator specializing in Spanish and Hebrew instruction, intercultural learning, and student identity. She taught for many years at Northwestern University and now lives in Beit Shemesh, Israel, where she continues teaching and writing.

title: Ethical leadership under constraint
summary: The post Ethical leadership under constraint appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Most conversations about ethical leadership begin with the leader. They ask what qualities ethical leaders have, how they make decisions, or what values they should embody. These are important questions, but they are incomplete.

Leadership is not only expressed through the character of individuals. It is expressed through the environments they create.

Every significant institutional decision changes the conditions into which the next decision will arrive. That simple observation has profound implications for higher education. Decisions do not end when committee papers are approved or organisational charts are updated. Every significant institutional decision has an afterlife. Long after the immediate outcome has faded, it continues shaping relationships, expectations and institutional culture.

Across the sector, universities are navigating financial uncertainty, organisational restructuring, increasing student need and heightened public scrutiny. Leaders are making difficult choices, often between competing goods rather than between obvious right and wrong. Constraint does not remove ethical responsibility. It reveals it. The question facing higher education is therefore not simply whether institutions can make difficult decisions. It is what those decisions will continue teaching people once the meeting has ended.

The gap between saying and doing

Every university publishes its values. They appear in strategic plans, recruitment materials, committee papers and institutional websites. They speak of collaboration, integrity, inclusion, academic freedom and respect. These aspirations matter because they communicate what an institution hopes to become. Yet values are not ultimately tested in publication. They are tested in practice. The defining question is whether those commitments remain recognisable when institutional interests begin competing with them.

The gap between stated values and enacted values rarely appears through dramatic failures of principle. More often, it emerges quietly through ordinary organisational processes. Consultation that arrives after the direction of travel has already been determined. Expertise that is acknowledged but carries little influence over outcomes. Transparency that consists of communication rather than meaningful participation. Procedural fairness that satisfies governance requirements while leaving those affected feeling unheard.

Few colleagues remember the wording of a strategic objective several years later. Many remember exactly how they experienced a consultation that reshaped their department, their workload or their students’ experience. Institutions are not experienced through the values they publish. They are experienced through the decisions people live.

The second history

Leadership literature often treats decisions as discrete events. Institutions experience them differently. Every significant institutional decision enters a university twice. First as an organisational decision. Then as a lived experience. The decision resolves an immediate question. The lived experience continues shaping how colleagues interpret the next consultation, the next restructuring, and the next institutional commitment. Whether people felt respected, whether disagreement genuinely had somewhere to go, whether expertise influenced the outcome, and whether uncertainty was acknowledged all become part of a wider institutional story.

Those stories rarely remain individual for long. They circulate between colleagues, across departments, through professional services and among successive student cohorts. Gradually they become institutional memory. Every new decision therefore enters an organisational environment already shaped by previous ones. Leaders are never making decisions on neutral ground. They are making them within an institutional ecology created by years of accumulated experience.

This ecological perspective changes how we think about leadership. Ethical leadership is not simply about making good decisions. It is about understanding that every decision reshapes the environment in which future decisions will be made. Leadership does not simply respond to institutional culture. Through everyday decisions it quietly creates the conditions from which future institutional culture will emerge.

Trust is not the destination

We often describe trust as something leaders build. I think trust is better understood as evidence. It is evidence that an institution has, over time, demonstrated sufficient consistency between what it says and what it repeatedly does. Universities are rarely judged by isolated moments. They are judged by patterns. Today’s decision will inevitably be interpreted alongside yesterday’s, and tomorrow’s decision will be understood through both.

Universities occupy a distinctive place in society because their legitimacy depends upon more than financial sustainability or regulatory compliance. Their authority rests upon a collective belief that they pursue education, knowledge and public benefit with intellectual integrity. Students are encouraged to question evidence, examine assumptions and evaluate competing claims. Staff devote their professional lives to those same principles. It is therefore unsurprising that both groups apply those habits of inquiry to the institutions in which they study and work. Universities do not become ethical because of the values they publish. They become ethical through the environments their decisions repeatedly create.

The ordinary work

Sometimes ethical leadership looks remarkably ordinary. It is explaining an unpopular decision with the same care as a popular one. It is inviting challenge before conclusions have been reached rather than afterwards. It is recognising that those closest to a problem frequently understand dimensions invisible from elsewhere in the organisation. It is acknowledging uncertainty without confusing certainty with competence. None of these actions appears transformational on its own. Collectively, they shape the institutional ecology that future colleagues and students will inherit.

Before the next decision

Before making significant organisational decisions, leaders might pause and ask themselves a different set of questions.

Does this decision strengthen or weaken the relationship between our stated values and our everyday practice?

Who has not yet been heard?

What assumptions am I making about how this decision will be experienced by others?

Beyond today’s outcome, what organisational conditions will this decision create?

What will today’s decisions teach tomorrow’s colleagues about what this institution truly values?

What future colleagues will find

Universities are rightly judged by the quality of their teaching, their research and their contribution to society. They should also be judged by something less visible but equally important: the environments they create through the accumulation of everyday decisions.

Leadership under constraint is often described as the challenge of making the least damaging decision. I think the challenge is different. Every institutional decision creates the conditions for the next. Ethical leadership is therefore not only about resolving today’s dilemma. It is about shaping the institutional environment that future colleagues and students will inherit.

What will today’s decisions teach tomorrow’s colleagues about what this institution truly values?

Dr Javeria Khadija Shah, SFHEA, is Senior Lecturer in Education and Inclusion and Associate Director of the Centre for Inclusive Pedagogy and Practice at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama, University of London. She is the originator of the ecology of whiteness framework and has published widely on race, identity, belonging and higher education. She is Founder and Creative Director of SUFIYANA CIC.

title: Lehrkräftebildung im KI-Zeitalter: Neue Ansätze für die Curricula des Lehramtsstudiums
summary:
Der Einzug von KI macht auch vor Schulen nicht halt. Aber wie werden angehende Lehrkräfte eigentlich darauf vorbereitet? In diesem Blogbeitrag zeigt Jannica Budde, was der aktuelle Stand von der Einbettung von KI in den Curricula ist, und stellt verschiedene Ansätze vor, wie der Erwerb von KI-Kompetenzen im Lehramtsstudium verankert werden kann.

The post Lehrkräftebildung im KI-Zeitalter: Neue Ansätze für die Curricula des Lehramtsstudiums appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Der Umgang mit Künstlicher Intelligenz und die Entwicklung entsprechender Kompetenzen sind spätestens seit der Einführung von ChatGPT und anderer generativer KI zu zentralen Themen für das Lehramtsstudium geworden. Bislang sind sie jedoch nur selten in den Studiengängen verankert. Dabei ist ein fachspezifischer Zugang zu KI notwendig – nicht nur im Lehramt. Ansätze aus den MINT-Fachdidaktiken zeigte eine gemeinsame Veranstaltung von Monitor Lehrkräftebildung und HFD am 28.05.2026.

ChatGPT und Co. machen auch vor den Schulen nicht halt. Doch wie sieht es aus mit der Förderung von KI-Kompetenzen bei (angehenden) Lehrkräften? Zwar gibt es an vielen Hochschulen fachübergreifende Angebote zum Erwerb von KI-Kompetenzen für Studierende (KI-Monitor 2025), wie das im Februar 2026 veröffentlichte Factsheet des Monitor Lehrkräftebildung zeigt, steht die flächendeckende Integration von KI-Kompetenzen im Lehramtsstudium jedoch noch am Anfang.

Nur rund ein Drittel der befragten Hochschulen gab an, dass der Umgang mit künstlicher Intelligenz im Wintersemester 2024/25 ein Querschnittsthema in allen Lehramtstypen sei, also in mehreren Lehrveranstaltungen bzw. Modulen des Lehramtsstudiums behandelt werde. Verpflichtende Angebote, in denen der Erwerb von Kompetenzen zum Umgang mit KI im Schulkontext ein Schwerpunktthema darstellt, gab es allerdings in allen Lehramtstypen nur an wenigen Hochschulen.

Bei der curricularen Verankerung von KI im Lehramt geht es nämlich nicht nur darum, generisches Wissen über KI zu vermitteln, sondern domänenspezifische KI-Kompetenzen zu fördern. Für das Lehramt bedeutet dies, u. a. den reflektierten Umgang mit KI-gestützten Lernumgebungen und die Integration KI-gestützter Werkzeuge in schulische Unterrichtskonzepte zu behandeln – und zwar jeweils fachbezogen (vgl. Müller & Buchholtz, 2026).

Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Professor für Digitale Bildung mit Schwerpunkt Künstlicher Intelligenz an der Universität zu Köln, und Nils Buchholtz, Professor für Didaktik der Mathematik – Sekundarstufe sowie Prodekan für Studium, Lehre und Prüfungswesen an der Universität Hamburg, zeigen in der Aufzeichnung des MLB-Talks, wie domänenspezifische KI-Kompetenzen in das Lehramtsstudium integriert werden können.

Künstliche Intelligenz bietet neue Gestaltungsmöglichkeiten für Lehr-/Lernprozesse in Schulen, etwa in Bezug auf die individuelle Förderung. Gleichzeitig besteht die Notwendigkeit, KI-Kompetenzen bei Schülern und Schülerinnen aller Fächer, Schulstufen und Schularten zu fördern. „Das heißt: Kein Fach kann sich hier ausnehmen. Keine Lehrkraft, egal in welchem Fach, kann sich hier davon befreien lassen, KI-Kompetenzen zu vermitteln”, betont Becker-Genschow in seinem Vortrag.

Die Beispiele aus Köln und Hamburg zeigen eindrücklich, wie die Integration von KI in den Lehramtsstudiengängen aussehen kann. Doch beide Referenten betonen ausdrücklich, dass KI-Kompetenz nicht nur allgemein, sondern auch fachspezifisch vermittelt werden muss. KI kommt im Deutsch- oder Englischunterricht anders zum Einsatz als in den Naturwissenschaften oder in der Mathematik.

Die Vermittlung KI-Kompetenzen geht dabei in allen Fällen über Handlungs- und Umsetzungskompetenzen hinaus. Ethische Fragen zum Umgang mit Datenschutz und geschlechtsspezifischen Bias von KI stehen daher auf dem Lehrplan beider Projekte. Sowohl Sebastian Becker-Genschow wie auch Nils Buchholtz heben in diesem Zusammenhang die Bedeutung von Haltung als wichtige Komponente der Kompetenzförderung hervor. „Die Studierenden sollen nach Möglichkeit eine gewisse Haltung zu KI entwickeln,” erläutert Buchholtz.

Insgesamt erscheint die curriculare Einbindung von KI im Lehramt zur Zeit jedoch nur sehr schleppend voranzukommen. Dies liegt laut Becker-Genschow und Buchholtz auch an den strukturellen Eigenheiten des Lehramts. So sind die Fachdidaktiken in der Regel den unterschiedlichen fachwissenschaftlichen Fakultäten zugeordnet und sind damit in der ganzen Universität verteilt. Hinzu kommt, dass es im Lehramt kaum Spielräume für curriculare Experimente gebe, so Buchholtz.

Schließlich gibt es überall noch Beharrungskräfte und große Unsicherheiten im Zusammenhang mit Künstlicher Intelligenz. Becker-Genschow empfiehlt seinen interessierten Kolleg:innen daher, Initiative zu zeigen. „Ich bin hoffnungsvoll, dass sich etwas tut”, so der Experte aus Köln.

translated_text:
Dealing with artificial intelligence and developing the corresponding skills have become central topics for teacher training since the introduction of ChatGPT and other generative AI. However, so far they have only rarely been anchored in the degree programs. A subject-specific approach to AI is necessary – not just in teaching. Approaches from MINT subject didactics were presented at a joint event by Monitor Teacher Education and HFD on May 28, 2026.

ChatGPT and Co. don’t stop at schools either. But what about promoting AI skills among (prospective) teachers? Although there are interdisciplinary offers at many universities for students to acquire AI skills (KI Monitor 2025), as the fact sheet from the Teacher Training Monitor published in February 2026 shows, the comprehensive integration of AI skills in teacher training courses is still in its early stages.

Only around a third of the universities surveyed stated that dealing with artificial intelligence in the winter semester of 2024/25 was a cross-sectional topic in all types of teacher training, i.e. that it was covered in several courses or modules of the teacher training course. However, only a few universities offered compulsory offers in which the acquisition of skills for dealing with AI in a school context was a key topic for all types of teaching qualifications.

The curricular anchoring of AI in teaching is not just about imparting generic knowledge about AI, but also about promoting domain-specific AI skills. For the teaching profession this means, among other things: to deal with the reflective use of AI-supported learning environments and the integration of AI-supported tools into school teaching concepts - in each case in a subject-specific manner (cf. Müller & Buchholtz, 2026).

Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Professor of Digital Education with a focus on Artificial Intelligence at the University of Cologne, and Nils Buchholtz, Professor of Didactics of Mathematics - Secondary School and Vice Dean for Studies, Teaching and Examination at the University of Hamburg, show in the recording of the MLB Talk how domain-specific AI skills can be integrated into teacher training.

Artificial intelligence offers new design options for teaching/learning processes in schools, for example in relation to individual support. At the same time, there is a need to promote AI skills among students of all subjects, school levels and types of schools. "That means: No subject can be exempt from this. No teacher, regardless of subject, can be exempt from teaching AI skills," emphasizes Becker-Genschow in his lecture.

The examples from Cologne and Hamburg impressively show what the integration of AI in teacher training courses can look like. However, both speakers expressly emphasize that AI competence must be taught not only in general, but also in a specific subject area. AI is used differently in German or English lessons than in natural sciences or mathematics.

In all cases, teaching AI skills goes beyond action and implementation skills. Ethical questions about how to deal with data protection and gender-specific bias in AI are therefore on the curriculum of both projects. In this context, both Sebastian Becker-Genschow and Nils Buchholtz emphasize the importance of attitude as an important component of promoting competence. “If possible, students should develop a certain attitude towards AI,” explains Buchholtz.

Overall, however, the curricular integration of AI in teaching appears to be making very slow progress at the moment. According to Becker-Genschow and Buchholtz, this is also due to the structural characteristics of the teaching profession. The subject didactics are usually assigned to the different subject faculties and are therefore distributed throughout the university. In addition, there is hardly any scope for curricular experiments in teaching, says Buchholtz.

After all, there are still forces of inertia and great uncertainty in connection with artificial intelligence everywhere. Becker-Genschow therefore recommends that his interested colleagues show initiative. “I am hopeful that something will happen,” said the expert from Cologne.

title: III Escuela de Posgrado de la Red de Estudios Sociales Latinoamericanos y Caribeños Contemporáneos
summary:
22 al 25 de Julio - Rio de Janeiro, Brasil

La entrada III Escuela de Posgrado de la Red de Estudios Sociales Latinoamericanos y Caribeños Contemporáneos se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
Con la participación de estudiantes de maestría y doctorado, docentes, investigadoras e investigadores, referentes de organizaciones sociales y responsables de políticas públicas de once países de América Latina y el Caribe, comenzó este 22 de julio en Río de Janeiro, Brasil, la III Escuela de Posgrado de la Red de Estudios Sociales Latinoamericanos y Caribeños Contemporáneos.

La Escuela es organizada por el Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales (CLACSO), la Asociación Latinoamericana de Sociología (ALAS) y la Red de Posgrados en Estudios Sociales Latinoamericanos (REDPEL), en coordinación con el Instituto de Estudios Sociales y Políticos de la Universidad del Estado de Río de Janeiro (IESP-UERJ), con el apoyo de la Fundação Lauro Campos e Marielle Franco y nueve programas de posgrado en ciencias sociales y sociología del estado de Río de Janeiro.

Bajo el lema «América Latina y el Caribe. Crisis y transformaciones: abordajes teóricos y metodológicos para el estudio social y político», esta tercera edición propone un espacio intensivo de formación orientado a fortalecer los proyectos de investigación de las y los participantes y a promover el diálogo entre la academia, las organizaciones sociales y las instituciones públicas desde una perspectiva crítica e interdisciplinaria.

Durante cuatro jornadas, la programación abordará algunos de los principales desafíos que atraviesan la región, con conferencias, paneles, coloquios y talleres metodológicos dedicados a la teoría social crítica, la dependencia económica y la soberanía, los movimientos sociales, la ecología política, las transiciones ecosociales, la geopolítica, los cuidados, los derechos humanos, las desigualdades, la inteligencia artificial y el capitalismo de plataformas, entre otros temas. Las actividades estarán a cargo de destacadas y destacados referentes de las ciencias sociales latinoamericanas y caribeñas.

En el saludo de apertura, el director ejecutivo de CLACSO, Pablo Vommaro, destacó que una Escuela Internacional de Posgrado es mucho más que un programa académico intensivo: constituye una experiencia de encuentro, convivencia y construcción colectiva de conocimiento que fortalece las redes de investigación y cooperación en la región. Asimismo, reafirmó el compromiso de CLACSO con una formación pública, crítica, interdisciplinaria y latinoamericanista, comprometida con la democracia, la justicia social y la integración de América Latina y el Caribe.

La III Escuela de Posgrado se desarrollará hasta el 25 de julio en las instalaciones del IESP-UERJ y concluirá con una actividad colectiva dedicada a debatir alternativas frente a la policrisis y los horizontes de cambio para la región.
